Actual Article Body:
Spokespeople come and go. The facts don’t change. Back independent journalism that answers to readers, not the podium. Become a HuffPost member today.

Already a member? Log in to hide these messages.

Follow the latest news on the major headlines of the day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to meet with President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss a deal to end his war on Ukraine, according to The Wall Street Journal.

And the proposed talks would reportedly not include Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

A former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter told the Journal that Putin first floated the idea to Trump during an Oct. 9 phone call when they worked out a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions about a potential summit were underway.

“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he said.

Read more in The Wall Street Journal:

CBS News legal correspondent Jan Crawford apologized and deleted a social media post supporting a heckler at a recent event for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

“Earlier, I tweeted a video from an Abdul El-Sayed town hall,” Crawford wrote in a Sunday social media statement. “I deleted that tweet because it was a violation of CBS News standards. I apologize.”

In her original tweet, Crawford thanked a man named Tommy for asking the Democrat to disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. She then criticized El-Sayed’s response.

“Sure. Yeah, absolutely,” El-Sayed said when Tommy posed the question. As HuffPost’s Kelby Vera reported, the Muslim Brotherhood is “a near-century old Islamist movement whose offshoots include both non-violent political factions and extremist groups like Hamas and al-Qaeda.”

El-Sayed also criticized the implication that he could have “dual loyalties.”

“Tommy, thank you. I had to watch this twice to catch Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s nanosecond ‘yeah absolutely’ response,” Crawford wrote. “His subsequent uninterrupted three-minute diatribe proving your exact point is the kind of spectacular self own most ppl only dream about triggering. Congrats.”

Crawford’s comments reportedly drew “internal backlash at CBS News,” according to The Guardian’s media reporter Jeremy Barr. The newsroom has also been scrutinized for its rightward shift during Bari Weiss’ tenure as editor-in-chief.

A CBS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Former President Barack Obama on Sunday condemned the Justice Department’s investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), describing it as an “appalling” example of the Trump administration targeting a lawmaker for her political positions.

“The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president,” Obama wrote in a social media statement.

“The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views,” he added.

The DOJ inquiry into Omar, which included a federal raid of her home, marks the latest instance of the Trump administration singling her out. For years, she’s faced racist attacks by the president and other Republicans.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, federal officials are scrutinizing Omar’s citizenship paperwork to build a case for denaturalizing her. The effort reportedly hinges on allegations that Omar was 18, and not a minor, when she was naturalized. Since Omar derived citizenship through her father’s application, she would have had to apply separately if she were an adult.

Omar has unequivocally denied the allegations, and officials previously found insufficient evidence to support similar claims during Trump’s first term, per The Washington Post.

“Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes. The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. Trump has also previously said that he had “nothing to do” with the search of Omar’s home.

DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Republican candidate for lieutenant governor in Massachusetts dropped out of the race on Sunday hours after he was arrested in a suspected drunk driving crash.

Shawn Oliver, a city councilor in New Bedford and a corrections officer, said in a post on X he was ending his campaign because “the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters.”

Read more from The Associated Press:

With just two weeks until Election Day, many Republican candidates are struggling to gain traction.

Gas prices are soaring in response to Donald Trump’s war on Iran. Food and other consumer goods are skyrocketing in price due to high energy costs and the president’s tariffs. The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate climbed above 7% this month, the highest level in nearly three years. And Trump’s response to this lack of affordability is to blame former President Joe Biden and urge voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Such a strategy seems poorly conceived.

For the past two years, the GOP has held power in the House, Senate and the White House, so there’s no one else to blame for rising inflation. A new Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll also shows the electorate has lost faith in the president. Trump’s approval rating fell to a new low of 33%, with 66% of respondents disapproving of the president, and 52% saying they strongly disapprove of him.

Even more worrying for the GOP, 71% of U.S. adults said they think the country is on the “wrong track,” which was the highest share yet in Trump’s second term. And for the first time in more than a decade, voters told pollsters they trust the Democrats to deal with the economy. In fact, if the election were held today, likely voters said they’d choose the Democratic congressional candidates over the Republican ones, 52% to 44%.

A member of the U.S. Air Force is dead after falling to the ground during a rappelling demonstration ahead of the U.S. Naval Academy’s football game against the University of Texas, San Antonio, on Saturday.

Witnesses said the airman was about half-way through a descent from the rafters of the Alamodome stadium when the service member began sliding down their rope in “an uncontrolled manner” and made hard impact with the ground.

The airman was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries and later confirmed dead by Air Force officials, who told military news outlet Task & Purpose that the incident is under investigation.

Officials did not identify the airman but confirmed they were a part of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 unit, which trains at Lackland Air Force Base, about 12 miles from where the incident happened.

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.

Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Read more here:

Canada’s defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire.

“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” Defense Minister David McGuinty said.

McGuinty did not provide casualty figures or details about what caused the incident. He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as “very, very active and delicate.”

Read more from The Associated Press:

An overwhelming majority of Arab Americans see a brighter future for themselves in the U.S., according to a Washington Post-Schar School poll, despite two-thirds who say they’re dissatisfied with the way things are going in the country.

Polling of this demographic is exceptionally rare. In order to be included in the survey, respondents had to confirm having ancestry in an Arab country as well as personally identify as Arab to be described as Arab American in the poll.

Those with ancestral roots across the Middle East and North Africa did not minimize the challenges or discrimination they face in the U.S.

For example, one in four reported they or a relative had struggled in the past two years with immigration issues, such as being questioned by airport security or having trouble entering or leaving the country.

But many held optimistic views about their quality of life and future. As a group, 78 percent said they have a good chance of improving their standard of living, compared with 40 percent of Americans overall.

And two-thirds of those surveyed say they consider themselves a “typical American,” and seven in 10 reported that being American is “very important” to their identity.

Read the full survey here.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.

Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Read more:

Several members of Congress condemned the Friday attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was beaten and severely injured by Israeli settlers while on assignment in the West Bank.

“The reported attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine by West Bank settlers is unconscionable and a moment of reckoning for the world,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) posted on X. “Are we going to tolerate accelerating vigilante violence against Palestinian civilians and foreign observers by right-wing vigilantes who operate with government protection?”

According to The Washington Post, Levine, a longtime photojournalist who has covered conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, was treated at a government hospital and suffered four broken vertebrae, a broken rib and lacerations throughout her body.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) also wrote on X that Israeli settlers “operate with impunity,” and urged the U.S. to “cut off aid to Israel that is used to fund settler activity, and stop the sales of these weapons.”

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia joins US President Donald Trump as he departs from the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 13, 2026.

"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," one Democratic strategist said. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”

The tumultuous tenure of White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has already come to an end just three days after her first press briefing.

After his new hire shambled her way through yet another Fox News appearance the night before, President Donald Trump said on Friday that he'd suggested Zacharia "reconsider" her role as the top White House spokesperson.

"Maybe it's not for her," Trump said, suggesting Zacharia may continue working for him “in some form, but maybe a more pleasant form.”

Zacharia, who stepped into the role formerly held by Karoline Leavitt, lasted a total of five days in the job. That's less than half the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci—who departed his role as White House communications director after just 11 days during Trump's first term.

Her qualifications were in doubt from the moment Trump plucked her from an obscure role as a Fox News commentator for the highly visible job. Journalists dug up old posts in which she promoted the QAnon and Pizzagate conspiracies, as well as Trump's false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

From the start of Zacharia's disastrous briefing on Tuesday, many observers predicted it could also be her last.

She was relentlessly panned after struggling to read through her fully scripted remarks (and at one point accidentally referring to her husband as "my president"). She cut the briefing short after just 14 minutes, taking only three questions, all from right-wing outlets.

It also became clear that, despite Trump's introduction of her as "an attorney," she'd never actually passed the bar exam and had misrepresented her credentials for years.

Asked by reporters earlier this week in which state she had passed the bar exam, she said, “When I moved to China" before later claiming not to have heard the question.

Even Fox News host Sean Hannity—a longtime Trump loyalist—challenged her explanation, confronting her Thursday with a report documenting “15 social media posts where you identify yourself as an attorney.”

“I think they were retweets,” Zacharia replied, arguing to a flummoxed Hannity that sharing the posts did not constitute endorsing the title.

While Zacharia's inability to do damage control appeared to do her in, Democratic strategist Mike Nellis emphasized that the problem was not her dishonesty—a trait that is practically a prerequisite to serve in the Trump administration.

"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," Nellis wrote on social media. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”

To some, Zacharia's tenure represented a disastrous culmination of Trump's willingness to eschew competence and experience for personal flattery and undying loyalty when appointing officials during his second term.

Zacharia said she got on Trump's radar by scheduling her TV appearances when she knew he'd be watching.

While other advisers questioned the pick, Zacharia's appointment was reportedly championed by Natalie Harp, Trump’s ever-present personal assistant and a fellow blonde conservative television personality.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on October 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"She looks nice for him," said former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Steele on MS NOW. "She fits his idea of the blonde white female standing at that podium publicly pronouncing his noise in a way that makes him, when he's watching it, feel good."

Steele emphasized that with just weeks left before a midterm election widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, "the White House is voiceless."

"They do not have a press secretary in place," he said, "because the president picked an incompetent individual to do the job."

Though very few seemed to think Zacharia could turn things around, she did have one person in her corner—perhaps the only other person who could possibly understand her experience: Scaramucci.

While others bet she would not even last "one Scaramucci," The Mooch himself predicted—even after her disastrous Hannity appearance on Thursday—that "she will make it. I have the over."

Following news on Friday that she did not, in fact, make it, Scaramucci wrote: "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Putin Wants To Ice Out Zelenskyy, Hold Peace Talks With Just Trump And Xi: Report

Actual Article Body:
Spokespeople come and go. The facts don’t change. Back independent journalism that answers to readers, not the podium. Become a HuffPost member today.

Already a member? Log in to hide these messages.

Follow the latest news on the major headlines of the day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to meet with President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss a deal to end his war on Ukraine, according to The Wall Street Journal.

And the proposed talks would reportedly not include Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

A former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter told the Journal that Putin first floated the idea to Trump during an Oct. 9 phone call when they worked out a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions about a potential summit were underway.

“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he said.

Read more in The Wall Street Journal:

CBS News legal correspondent Jan Crawford apologized and deleted a social media post supporting a heckler at a recent event for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

“Earlier, I tweeted a video from an Abdul El-Sayed town hall,” Crawford wrote in a Sunday social media statement. “I deleted that tweet because it was a violation of CBS News standards. I apologize.”

In her original tweet, Crawford thanked a man named Tommy for asking the Democrat to disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. She then criticized El-Sayed’s response.

“Sure. Yeah, absolutely,” El-Sayed said when Tommy posed the question. As HuffPost’s Kelby Vera reported, the Muslim Brotherhood is “a near-century old Islamist movement whose offshoots include both non-violent political factions and extremist groups like Hamas and al-Qaeda.”

El-Sayed also criticized the implication that he could have “dual loyalties.”

“Tommy, thank you. I had to watch this twice to catch Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s nanosecond ‘yeah absolutely’ response,” Crawford wrote. “His subsequent uninterrupted three-minute diatribe proving your exact point is the kind of spectacular self own most ppl only dream about triggering. Congrats.”

Crawford’s comments reportedly drew “internal backlash at CBS News,” according to The Guardian’s media reporter Jeremy Barr. The newsroom has also been scrutinized for its rightward shift during Bari Weiss’ tenure as editor-in-chief.

A CBS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Former President Barack Obama on Sunday condemned the Justice Department’s investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), describing it as an “appalling” example of the Trump administration targeting a lawmaker for her political positions.

“The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president,” Obama wrote in a social media statement.

“The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views,” he added.

The DOJ inquiry into Omar, which included a federal raid of her home, marks the latest instance of the Trump administration singling her out. For years, she’s faced racist attacks by the president and other Republicans.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, federal officials are scrutinizing Omar’s citizenship paperwork to build a case for denaturalizing her. The effort reportedly hinges on allegations that Omar was 18, and not a minor, when she was naturalized. Since Omar derived citizenship through her father’s application, she would have had to apply separately if she were an adult.

Omar has unequivocally denied the allegations, and officials previously found insufficient evidence to support similar claims during Trump’s first term, per The Washington Post.

“Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes. The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. Trump has also previously said that he had “nothing to do” with the search of Omar’s home.

DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Republican candidate for lieutenant governor in Massachusetts dropped out of the race on Sunday hours after he was arrested in a suspected drunk driving crash.

Shawn Oliver, a city councilor in New Bedford and a corrections officer, said in a post on X he was ending his campaign because “the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters.”

Read more from The Associated Press:

With just two weeks until Election Day, many Republican candidates are struggling to gain traction.

Gas prices are soaring in response to Donald Trump’s war on Iran. Food and other consumer goods are skyrocketing in price due to high energy costs and the president’s tariffs. The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate climbed above 7% this month, the highest level in nearly three years. And Trump’s response to this lack of affordability is to blame former President Joe Biden and urge voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Such a strategy seems poorly conceived.

For the past two years, the GOP has held power in the House, Senate and the White House, so there’s no one else to blame for rising inflation. A new Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll also shows the electorate has lost faith in the president. Trump’s approval rating fell to a new low of 33%, with 66% of respondents disapproving of the president, and 52% saying they strongly disapprove of him.

Even more worrying for the GOP, 71% of U.S. adults said they think the country is on the “wrong track,” which was the highest share yet in Trump’s second term. And for the first time in more than a decade, voters told pollsters they trust the Democrats to deal with the economy. In fact, if the election were held today, likely voters said they’d choose the Democratic congressional candidates over the Republican ones, 52% to 44%.

A member of the U.S. Air Force is dead after falling to the ground during a rappelling demonstration ahead of the U.S. Naval Academy’s football game against the University of Texas, San Antonio, on Saturday.

Witnesses said the airman was about half-way through a descent from the rafters of the Alamodome stadium when the service member began sliding down their rope in “an uncontrolled manner” and made hard impact with the ground.

The airman was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries and later confirmed dead by Air Force officials, who told military news outlet Task & Purpose that the incident is under investigation.

Officials did not identify the airman but confirmed they were a part of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 unit, which trains at Lackland Air Force Base, about 12 miles from where the incident happened.

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.

Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Read more here:

Canada’s defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire.

“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” Defense Minister David McGuinty said.

McGuinty did not provide casualty figures or details about what caused the incident. He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as “very, very active and delicate.”

Read more from The Associated Press:

An overwhelming majority of Arab Americans see a brighter future for themselves in the U.S., according to a Washington Post-Schar School poll, despite two-thirds who say they’re dissatisfied with the way things are going in the country.

Polling of this demographic is exceptionally rare. In order to be included in the survey, respondents had to confirm having ancestry in an Arab country as well as personally identify as Arab to be described as Arab American in the poll.

Those with ancestral roots across the Middle East and North Africa did not minimize the challenges or discrimination they face in the U.S.

For example, one in four reported they or a relative had struggled in the past two years with immigration issues, such as being questioned by airport security or having trouble entering or leaving the country.

But many held optimistic views about their quality of life and future. As a group, 78 percent said they have a good chance of improving their standard of living, compared with 40 percent of Americans overall.

And two-thirds of those surveyed say they consider themselves a “typical American,” and seven in 10 reported that being American is “very important” to their identity.

Read the full survey here.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.

Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Read more:

Several members of Congress condemned the Friday attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was beaten and severely injured by Israeli settlers while on assignment in the West Bank.

“The reported attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine by West Bank settlers is unconscionable and a moment of reckoning for the world,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) posted on X. “Are we going to tolerate accelerating vigilante violence against Palestinian civilians and foreign observers by right-wing vigilantes who operate with government protection?”

According to The Washington Post, Levine, a longtime photojournalist who has covered conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, was treated at a government hospital and suffered four broken vertebrae, a broken rib and lacerations throughout her body.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) also wrote on X that Israeli settlers “operate with impunity,” and urged the U.S. to “cut off aid to Israel that is used to fund settler activity, and stop the sales of these weapons.”

"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," one Democratic strategist said. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”

The tumultuous tenure of White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has already come to an end just three days after her first press briefing.

After his new hire shambled her way through yet another Fox News appearance the night before, President Donald Trump said on Friday that he'd suggested Zacharia "reconsider" her role as the top White House spokesperson.

"Maybe it's not for her," Trump said, suggesting Zacharia may continue working for him “in some form, but maybe a more pleasant form.”

Zacharia, who stepped into the role formerly held by Karoline Leavitt, lasted a total of five days in the job. That's less than half the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci—who departed his role as White House communications director after just 11 days during Trump's first term.

Her qualifications were in doubt from the moment Trump plucked her from an obscure role as a Fox News commentator for the highly visible job. Journalists dug up old posts in which she promoted the QAnon and Pizzagate conspiracies, as well as Trump's false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

From the start of Zacharia's disastrous briefing on Tuesday, many observers predicted it could also be her last.

She was relentlessly panned after struggling to read through her fully scripted remarks (and at one point accidentally referring to her husband as "my president"). She cut the briefing short after just 14 minutes, taking only three questions, all from right-wing outlets.

It also became clear that, despite Trump's introduction of her as "an attorney," she'd never actually passed the bar exam and had misrepresented her credentials for years.

Asked by reporters earlier this week in which state she had passed the bar exam, she said, “When I moved to China" before later claiming not to have heard the question.

Even Fox News host Sean Hannity—a longtime Trump loyalist—challenged her explanation, confronting her Thursday with a report documenting “15 social media posts where you identify yourself as an attorney.”

“I think they were retweets,” Zacharia replied, arguing to a flummoxed Hannity that sharing the posts did not constitute endorsing the title.

While Zacharia's inability to do damage control appeared to do her in, Democratic strategist Mike Nellis emphasized that the problem was not her dishonesty—a trait that is practically a prerequisite to serve in the Trump administration.

"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," Nellis wrote on social media. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”

To some, Zacharia's tenure represented a disastrous culmination of Trump's willingness to eschew competence and experience for personal flattery and undying loyalty when appointing officials during his second term.

Zacharia said she got on Trump's radar by scheduling her TV appearances when she knew he'd be watching.

While other advisers questioned the pick, Zacharia's appointment was reportedly championed by Natalie Harp, Trump’s ever-present personal assistant and a fellow blonde conservative television personality.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on October 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"She looks nice for him," said former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Steele on MS NOW. "She fits his idea of the blonde white female standing at that podium publicly pronouncing his noise in a way that makes him, when he's watching it, feel good."

Steele emphasized that with just weeks left before a midterm election widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, "the White House is voiceless."

"They do not have a press secretary in place," he said, "because the president picked an incompetent individual to do the job."

Though very few seemed to think Zacharia could turn things around, she did have one person in her corner—perhaps the only other person who could possibly understand her experience: Scaramucci.

While others bet she would not even last "one Scaramucci," The Mooch himself predicted—even after her disastrous Hannity appearance on Thursday—that "she will make it. I have the over."

Following news on Friday that she did not, in fact, make it, Scaramucci wrote: "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."
